title: A Generalized Unified Character Code: Western European and CJK Sections
summary: An April 1st joke RFC describing a fully unified coded character set for Latin, Greek, Cyrillic, and CJK-based scripts. It is not a complete specification. It is informational and humorous.

plainLanguage.summary: This joke paper suggests mashing many alphabets together into one big set of letters. It is not meant seriously.

questions: how does this character code work
subtitle: A unified character code combining Latin, Greek, Cyrillic, and CJK (April 1st satire)

tldr.problem: This April 1st RFC presents a humorous alternative to Unicode, arguing that unified character sets for internationalized domain names need radical re-thinking. The joke proposes combining Latin, Greek, Cyrillic, and CJK scripts into a single encoding with unconventional rules.
tldr.mechanism: The document defines character types (base characters, nonspacing marks, case indicators, joining indicators, positioning indicators), assigns 23-bit code values, and invents rules for canonical form that result in absurd encodings: uppercase A is coded as a plus UC, and w doesn't exist but is u plus ZWCJ plus u.
tldr.outcome: This is an April 1st joke RFC published in 2008. It is not a serious proposal and was never implemented. The IESG note explicitly disclaims it as an IETF document.

facts.label: Code width
facts.value: 23 bits (chosen because 3 and 23 are prime, unlike 42)

today: RFC 5242 is an April 1st joke RFC that was never implemented. It remains a humorous critique of over-complicated internationalization schemes. The real standard for international text remains Unicode, which takes a far more pragmatic approach.

sections.title: A Radical Approach to Unified Encoding
sections.content:
RFC 5242 is published on 1 April 2008 as a humorous alternative to Unicode. The IESG note warns that this is not an IETF document and the RFC Editor included it "at its discretion." The document describes a "fully unified coded character set for scripts based on Latin, Greek, Cyrillic, and Chinese characters."

The proposal is guided by four whimsical principles: (1) if glyphs look alike, treat them alike; (2) if symbols mean the same thing, encode them identically; (3) prefer sanserif fonts; (4) use combining characters and modifiers rather than adding base characters. These principles lead to consequences Unicode designers never imagined.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of Unicode's sensible design, this joke proposes mashing all alphabets together with weird construction rules.

sections.title: Character Construction Rules
sections.content:
The spec defines several character types: Base Characters (atomic shapes like 'a'), Nonspacing Marks (combining dots and hooks), Case Indicators (the UC modifier, code value 1 hex, so uppercase A is the lowercase letter a combined with the UC marker), and Joining Indicators (ZWCJ, OJ, ONJ, ZWJ, ZWNJ). The document then defines Positioning Indicators (PositionLeft, PositionCenter, and others) and Repetition Indicators (Repeat2, Repeat3).

The result is absurdist: the letter b is the character o combined with VerticalLine and PositionLeft; d is o combined with VerticalLine and PositionRight. And (as a punchline) there is no w—it is constructed as u combined with ZWCJ combined with u. The Catalan ligature becomes l combined with ZWCJ, a period, PositionVMiddle, and ZWCJ, then l again.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of having a letter for every character, you build letters from smaller pieces. Uppercase letters are just lowercase with a tag. The lowercase 'w' doesn't exist; you make it from two 'u's joined together.

sections.title: The Encoding Scheme
sections.content:
Code values occupy exactly 23 bits ("unlike 42"), a joke reference to Douglas Adams' Hitchhiker's Guide. Values 1-255 are reserved for modifiers, 256-511 for combining marks, 512-1023 for "general principles," and 1024+ for actual characters. The document mandates a "shortest string" canonical form rule: if two representations exist, the shorter one wins; if tied, the one with the smaller octet sum is correct. Any deviation is invalid.

The mailing list for questions is a fake internationalized domain name: "unified-ccs@xn--iwem3b1f.xn--90ase1a.bogus.domain.name."
sections.plainLanguage: Characters get code numbers using 23 bits. When you write a character multiple ways, only the shortest way is correct. If the shortest ways are the same length, you pick the one with the smallest numbers.

sections.title: Why This Is Satire
sections.content:
The RFC is presented entirely seriously, with sections on "Examples of Graphic Element Codes" (Section 5) and "Composite Characters and Unicode Equivalences" (Section 6). But the design is deliberately impractical: the complexity of rules for combining characters, the arbitrary 23-bit choice, and the contrived positioning system are jokes at the expense of over-complicated specifications.

The IESG note explicitly states this is not IETF work and that the RFC Editor chose to publish it for humor. It is classified Informational, not Standards Track.
sections.plainLanguage: The whole thing is written in serious RFC language, but the system is so complicated and weird that nobody would ever use it. That's the joke.

references.text: The Unicode Consortium, The Unicode Standard, Version 5.0, Addison-Wesley Professional, 2006.
